contributions: Effective Token Cost (ETC), a platform-agnostic metric weighting non-cached input, cached input, and output tokens to compare efficiency-effectiveness tradeoffs across deep-search configurations under both hardware-cost and API-pricing regimes
a systematic study, using a controlled retrieval corpus (BrowseComp-Plus), of how model scale, reasoning effort, and reranking depth jointly determine deep-search agent efficiency and effectiveness

an empirical finding that allocating test-time budget to listwise reranking depth is generally more cost-effective than increasing agent reasoning effort, with moderate reranking depth plus moderate reasoning matching high-reasoning-effort accuracy at substantially lower cost

a generalization of ETC to heterogeneous agent/reranker model pairings, showing a lightweight cross-encoder reranker retains most of listwise reranking's end-to-end accuracy gain while further reducing cost, in part because listwise reranking's sliding-window procedure at high depth incurs redundant document reprocessing overhead the cross-encoder avoids
limitations: Experiments focus specifically on the gpt-oss model family (chosen because reasoning effort is controllable via system prompts); the paper's own limitations note extending to commercial models with controllable reasoning effort would strengthen generality of the findings. Experiments use BrowseComp-Plus's fixed, human-verified retrieval corpus rather than live web search, so results may not fully transfer to settings relying on external, less-controlled search APIs. Reranking is implemented as a fixed top-d selection at each step; the paper notes a learned relevance model that adaptively selects a variable-sized subset could better filter redundant or irrelevant context, which is not explored. Due to compute limits, each configuration is run only once (cross-run variance is separately analyzed in an appendix) rather than averaged over multiple runs.
method: Uses the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark (a fixed, human-verified retrieval corpus enabling controlled analysis, 830 deep-search queries) with qwen3-embedding-8b as the base retriever. Defines Effective Token Cost (ETC = Input_nc + alpha*Input_c + beta*Output_t) accounting for cached vs. non-cached input tokens (weighted by a caching discount alpha reflecting prefix-reuse efficiency) and output/reasoning tokens (weighted by a premium beta reflecting their higher generation cost), enabling platform-agnostic comparison of efficiency-effectiveness tradeoffs across configurations. Studies gpt-oss-20b and gpt-oss-120b as search agents under low/medium/high reasoning-effort settings (varied via system prompts, since these models lack a toggleable thinking mode), each optionally paired with a zero-shot listwise reranker (RankLLM, window size 20) operating over reranking depths d in {10,20,50} before the final top-5 documents are passed to the agent. Evaluates both a one-shot retrieval-reranking setting (isolating reranking quality via NDCG/Recall against evidence/gold documents) and the full end-to-end deep-search pipeline (Accuracy via LLM-as-judge, Recall, number of search calls, Calibration Error). Extends the analysis to a heterogeneous setup using qwen3-reranker-0.6b as a lightweight cross-encoder reranker (binary yes/no relevance judged via the logit of the 'yes' token), generalizing ETC to ETC = ETC_agent + gamma*ETC_reranker where gamma reflects the smaller reranker's relative inference FLOPs (0.32 for qwen3-reranker-0.6b vs. gpt-oss-20b).
one_liner: Introduces Effective Token Cost (ETC), a hardware/pricing-aware metric weighting cached vs. non-cached input and output tokens, to study how deep-search agents should allocate test-time budget between listwise document reranking depth and agent reasoning effort -- finding moderate reranking depth is consistently more cost-effective than increasing search-time reasoning, and that a lightweight cross-encoder reranker recovers most of listwise reranking's end-to-end accuracy gain at substantially lower cost.
problem: Deep-research agents that iteratively retrieve and reason to answer complex queries face significant efficiency concerns as test-time computation scales, but the specific role of listwise reranking -- standard in information-retrieval systems but underexplored in agentic multi-turn search -- and its interaction with, and cost-effectiveness relative to, increased agent reasoning effort has not been systematically studied, partly because many prior evaluations rely on opaque web search APIs that conflate retrieval quality with external service behavior.

relevance.overthinking: Indirectly relevant: this is about test-time compute allocation in agentic retrieval-augmented search (reranking depth vs. reasoning effort), not single-trace reasoning-length overthinking, but its central empirical finding -- that a fixed test-time compute budget is often better spent on a different lever (retrieval quality) than on more reasoning tokens, with reasoning-effort gains showing comparatively weaker cost-efficiency -- generalizes the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff question this archive tracks beyond single-model reasoning length to multi-component agentic pipelines, and its ETC metric is a reusable, more realistic cost accounting than raw token count for any efficiency comparison in this archive that spans cached vs. non-cached or input vs. output tokens.

results: In the one-shot reranking setting, oss-120b consistently outperforms oss-20b as a listwise reranker across all depths and reasoning budgets, with effectiveness improving monotonically with reranking depth d for both models (e.g. oss-120b at medium reasoning reaches NDCG@5=46.05 at d=50, its best result); increasing reasoning budget improves ranking quality for both models but gives larger gains for oss-20b, especially at higher d where ranking is harder. Per-effective-token-cost analysis (Recall@5 gain per 1M ETC tokens) shows increasing reranking depth d has a much stronger effect than increasing reasoning effort within a fixed d: moving from d=10 to d=20 yields 5-7 NDCG points, with a further 3.5-10 points from d=20 to d=50, whereas raising reasoning effort at fixed d yields comparatively modest gains -- so much so that oss-120b at medium reasoning with a given d can still underperform oss-20b at low reasoning at the next higher d level. In the full end-to-end deep-research pipeline, for fixed model size and reranking depth, increasing reasoning effort consistently improves both recall and accuracy, with larger gains for oss-20b than oss-120b (e.g. oss-20b with high reasoning can be more effective than oss-120b with low reasoning, underscoring reasoning-budget importance relative to raw model scale); for fixed model size and reasoning effort, increasing d improves both recall and accuracy, though under high reasoning at d=50 the two models differ by under 3 recall points but about 7 accuracy points, suggesting oss-20b is comparatively less effective at converting improved retrieval into correct final answers than oss-120b is. Increasing d only slightly reduces the number of search calls (up to 12% for oss-120b-high at d=50 vs. d=0), indicating reranking's accuracy improvements stem primarily from better retrieved-document quality rather than changed agentic search behavior. Accuracy-per-ETC analysis confirms reranking yields strong gains for both models: under low reasoning, increasing depth from d=0 to d in {10,20,50} gives large accuracy improvements at modest additional ETC; under medium/high reasoning, gains persist for d<=20 but show diminishing returns from d=20 to d=50; for each model, medium reasoning combined with deeper reranking matches high-reasoning performance with shallow/no reranking at substantially lower ETC -- directly demonstrating that allocating budget to reranking is often more cost-effective than increasing search-agent reasoning effort, especially for the larger model. Latency analysis shows moderate reasoning with moderate reranking depth provides the most favorable practical tradeoff, being substantially faster than high reasoning while still improving end-to-end accuracy and reducing ETC; latency increases with reranking depth under low/medium reasoning but actually decreases under high reasoning (driven by fewer search calls). In the heterogeneous setup, the lightweight cross-encoder reranker (qwen3-reranker-0.6b) still improves end-to-end accuracy and recall over no reranking, though with smaller gains than the full listwise setup (e.g. oss-20b-high at d=50: 52.91% accuracy / 66.63% recall for the cross-encoder vs. 55.97% / 71.29% for listwise reranking); since the cross-encoder's relative inference cost gamma is well under 1, it is shown to be substantially more cost-effective per ETC than listwise reranking despite achieving slightly lower peak accuracy -- and listwise reranking's relative cost disadvantage worsens further at d=50 specifically because its sliding-window procedure causes each document to be redundantly re-processed (~1.6x on average), an overhead the cross-encoder does not incur.
